summary: The Greek debt negotiations collapsed over the final days of the window: after the ECB froze/capped emergency liquidity to Greek banks, the government called a referendum on the creditors' bailout terms, eurozone finance ministers refused to extend talks past the deadline, and Greece imposed bank closures and ATM withdrawal limits while shutting the Athens Exchange. A second, reinforcing sovereign-credit shock came from Puerto Rico's governor declaring the island's $72 billion of debt 'not payable'.
mechanism: Capital controls, a shuttered national exchange and an explicit referendum on bailout terms create binary, headline-driven repricing of sovereign and bank credit and of currency-union redenomination risk, which propagates into cross-asset volatility; a simultaneous large municipal-debt repudiation broadens the credit-risk repricing.

claims.claim: The ECB had earlier been raising the cap on emergency liquidity assistance to Greek banks as depositors withdrew over 3 billion euros.
Talks appeared to be moving toward a deal mid-window when the Greek prime minister offered new reforms, but a senior parliamentary figure warned the body might reject the concessions.
The Greek prime minister announced a referendum on the creditors' bailout deal, which parliament then approved.
Eurozone finance ministers rejected Greece's request to extend debt negotiations past the deadline.
The ECB was reported to be capping lending to Greek banks, worsening the bank run, with a referendum pending on euro membership.
Greece closed its banks with ATM withdrawal limits and shut the Athens Exchange as financial conditions worsened.
The Governor of Puerto Rico said the territory's debts are 'not payable' and that it cannot pay off $72 billion of debt.
The People's Bank of China cut interest rates for a fourth successive time to help stabilise growth.

competing_explanation: A cluster of high-casualty attacks on the same day (a beach resort in Tunisia, a Shia mosque in Kuwait, a factory attack near Lyon) could be read as a geopolitical risk shock, and a Chinese central bank rate cut signals growth concerns; but neither has the direct, mechanical link to funding markets and exchange closure that the Greek events do.
